title: New movements
hook: lay movements like Focolare and Sant'Egidio work for unity and peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catholics under pressure today: a bishop sent into exile, a parish attacked at Mass, names said aloud. Your line was not only long ago. Whose name or town did you say? Day nine hundred forty-five.

Trent, in northern Italy, during the Second World War. The bombs are falling, and a young schoolteacher named Chiara Lubich crowds into an air-raid shelter with a few friends. They've brought one book, the Gospels, and they read it by candlelight, asking what would still stand if everything else fell. They keep landing on Jesus's prayer that his followers may all be one. Years later, in Rome, a group of high school students starts meeting to read the Gospel and then going out to the poor on the edge of the city. Neither group was started by a bishop or a priest. Today is what grew out of rooms like those.
screen: `A BOMB SHELTER IN TRENT.` → `ONE BOOK BY CANDLELIGHT.` → `STUDENTS IN ROME.`

segments.voice: First, Focolare. Chiara's circle became the Focolare movement. Focolare is Italian for hearth, the fire a family gathers around, and that was the idea: small communities living the Gospel together like a family at the fire. Their key text is Jesus's prayer at the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee." Focolare took it to heart, building friendships with other Christians, with people of other faiths, and with people of none. Second, Sant'Egidio. The Roman students, gathered by Andrea Riccardi, took their name from a small church in the Trastevere neighborhood. Their life rests on three things: prayer each evening, friendship with the poor, and peace. That last one reached all the way to a war: talks held at their house in Rome helped bring the civil war in Mozambique to an end. Third, who leads. These movements are led by laypeople, people who aren't priests or vowed religious, with jobs and families. The Second Vatican Council taught that the laity share in the Church's mission by their own calling, through baptism, not as helpers on loan from the clergy. Movements like these are one shape that teaching took. Priests and bishops belong to some of them, but the founders were a teacher and a student. Fourth, the week. Look back over it: a pope greeting the world with peace, a teenager with a website, pilgrims walking, a church on every continent, a church underground, believers under pressure. And now laypeople leading. One Church, seen through different doors.
screen: `FOCOLARE: A HEARTH.` · `SANT'EGIDIO: PRAYER, THE POOR, PEACE.` · `THE LAITY SHARE THE MISSION.` · `ONE CHURCH THROUGH DIFFERENT DOORS.` · then, large: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a lay movement near you. Settle, and breathe. Think of the place where you live. Somewhere near it there may be laypeople already at work: a parish group running a food pantry, a prayer circle in someone's living room, a Saint Vincent de Paul group collecting coats, a Focolare or Sant'Egidio community, a Catholic Worker house. Let one come to mind, or decide what you'd look for. Choose one to look up after the bell. Then rest your hands in your lap and notice what they could carry for an hour a week. If you pray, you can ask where they're needed. If you don't, let the question sit quietly. The bell holds the time.
New movements. Communities like Focolare and Sant'Egidio, started and led by laypeople, working for unity, for the poor and for peace.
Your line: laypeople lead. Today, look up the one group you chose and find out when it next meets. Day nine hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics join lay movements and associations such as Focolare, Sant'Egidio and the Saint Vincent de Paul Society, meeting for prayer and Scripture and serving the poor, usually alongside their parish life.
